chef_bio.background: SUKE6 DINER opened in March 2015 on the corner of Sukeroku Yume-dōri, a cherry-tree-lined street along the Sumida River embankment in Asakusa — the street's name is where the restaurant's name comes from. The building is a renovated former footwear-wholesaler warehouse; the diner occupies the 1st and 2nd floors, while the 3rd floor houses an in-house bakery workshop called "Manufacture" that bakes the bread served downstream and sells baked goods on weekends. It is run by Epietriz Inc. , which also operates a few other concept cafés in Tokyo.
chef_bio.philosophy: The restaurant's guiding concept is "EAT GOOD" — food they would be happy to serve their own families, without chemical seasonings. Beyond sourcing organic/low-pesticide produce, the kitchen makes as much as possible in house: bacon, sausage and other charcuterie, salad dressing, ginger ale and lemonade are all handmade rather than bought in.
chef_bio.specialty: Avocado toast and the skillet-served English breakfast are among its best-known dishes, alongside a signature burger ("Sukeroku Burger") and a weekday morning set.

anecdotes.text: Owner Matsuura, who lives in Hayama, personally drives Miura-peninsula vegetables and local farm eggs to the restaurant most mornings; the shop also draws seasonal produce from contracted farms in Kyushu and from Epietriz's own farm in Yamanashi.

About 40% of the diner's customers are visitors from overseas; the bilingual (Japanese/English) menu and social posts reflect a stated aim of making the space welcoming to everyone regardless of nationality, age, or gender.
The diner's concept of hand-making processed foods and seasonings in-house, down to condiments, was covered as part of Epietriz's "EAT GOOD" philosophy at the restaurant's 2015 opening.

chef_bio.background: Tomita Shoten occupies a bookstore building from the early Showa era in Kanda-Misakicho, a short walk from Suidobashi Station. In 2017 the old bookshop was renovated into a charcoal-grill bistro by architect Kuma Taichi, son of renowned architect Kengo Kuma, who kept the wooden bookshelves and warm, mid-century atmosphere while turning the space into a restaurant. It is run by the local company Nasuya (owner Mitsufuji Kimihisa), which also operates the nearby motsu-dining spot Umakamon in Suidobashi.
chef_bio.philosophy: The concept ties the space's former life as a bookstore to the menu: each table is given a picture book that doubles as part of the menu, and diners can order dishes inspired by scenes from beloved stories, paired with charcoal-grilled seasonal produce and meats and natural wine in a renovated, book-lined dining room.
chef_bio.specialty: Charcoal-grilled wagyu sirloin steak, and the restaurant's signature concept of recreating dishes that appear in famous books, manga, and anime (e. g. Sanji's crispy potato paille from One Piece, the meatball spaghetti from Lupin III: The Castle of Cagliostro, and the castella pancake from the picture book Guri and Gura), served alongside seasonal charcoal-grilled vegetables and a rotating natural wine list.

anecdotes.text: The building is a renovated early-Showa-era bookstore in Suidobashi/Misakicho, redesigned in 2017 by architect Kuma Taichi (son of Kengo Kuma), preserving a book-lined, mid-century interior.

Each table's menu takes the form of a picture book, and diners can order the actual dish described in that book's story — e.g. Sanji's crispy potato paille (One Piece), the meatball spaghetti from Lupin III: The Castle of Cagliostro, and a castella pancake inspired by Guri and Gura.
The restaurant is operated by Nasuya, a small Chiyoda-based hospitality company owned by Mitsufuji Kimihisa, which also runs the motsu-dining izakaya Umakamon near Suidobashi.

cultural_comfort.note: A Japanese-concept restaurant (book-themed charcoal-grill bistro) with no confirmation of an English menu or English-speaking staff, though it appears on English-language Tabelog and online reservation platforms; basic Japanese or a translation app is useful for describing dietary restrictions.

chef_bio.background: Ramen Nagi began in 2004 as a tiny 8-seat, one-day-a-week shop in Shinjuku's Golden Gai, founded by Fukuoka-born chef Satoshi Ikuta. In 2006 the company launched its tonkotsu (pork-bone) sub-brand, Butao, and this Shibuya location opened June 15, 2006 (renewed/reopened March 2, 2020). Butao later became an unexpected overseas hit as 'BUTAO' after opening a flagship in Hong Kong's Central district in 2010, and that overseas popularity helped cement its reputation back in Japan.
chef_bio.philosophy: The kitchen's stated aim with the tonkotsu broth is to avoid the heavy, off-putting pork-bone odor common to the style while still delivering concentrated flavor, resulting in a broth that finishes lighter than its richness would suggest.

chef_bio.background: The building has been in the Imoto family's book trade since her grandfather founded Kitazawa Bookstore here in 1902, later run as a foreign-language bookstore by her father. A children's picture-book shop called "Bookhouse Jimbocho" occupied the same spot from 2007-2017 with backing from major publishers, but closed in 2017 once it was felt to have fulfilled its cultural role. Yoshiko Imoto, who had raised her own children on visits to that shop, felt Jimbocho (Tokyo's famous book district) could not be allowed to lose its only picture-book specialist, and took over the business herself despite doubts from family, friends and neighboring booksellers. She reopened it as Book House Cafe on May 5, 2017, built on four pillars -- bookstore, cafe, events, and rentable gallery/event space -- to keep it financially sustainable.
chef_bio.philosophy: Keep Jimbocho's only new-picture-book specialty store alive as a place where people connect over books, pairing over 10,000 picture books with a cafe, an evening picture-book bar ("Liliput"), and gallery/event space for readings and exhibitions.
chef_bio.specialty: Beef and cheese curry made with roux from a well-known Jimbocho curry shop, plus a house baked curry-bread and hayashi rice; it has been entered in the Kanda Curry Grand Prix.

anecdotes.text: During the COVID-19 pandemic, when business was in serious difficulty, Imoto posted a direct, crowdfunding-style appeal for support on the shop's own website, and customers rallied to help the store survive.
The shop occupies the site of the earlier publisher-backed picture-book store "Bookhouse Jimbocho" (2007-2017); Imoto took over rather than let Jimbocho lose its only picture-book specialist.

tokyo_chompoo.notes: Chef Kan Morieda trained at Tetsuya's in Sydney, at the Kyoto kaiseki restaurant Kogetsu (湖月), and at the molecular-gastronomy Tapas Molecular Bar inside the Mandarin Oriental Tokyo, before going independent in 2011 and later opening CHOMPOO in Shibuya PARCO in November 2019.

chef_bio.philosophy: An additive-free, MSG-free take on Thai food built on generous use of fresh herbs and spices — described by the chef's team as not 'Thailand's first Thai food' nor 'just spicy', but a comforting, deeply flavorful ('しみじみおいしい') style of Thai cooking, with colorful, photogenic plating.
chef_bio.specialty: カオヤム (Kao Yam) — a vividly blue butterfly-pea-rice herb salad that has become the restaurant's signature, widely shared on social media.

anecdotes.text: CHOMPOO opened in November 2019 on the 4th floor of Shibuya PARCO as one of the dining anchors of the rebuilt mall, produced by chef Kan Morieda (who also ran Shimokitazawa's Salmon and Trout).
The restaurant has run seasonal menu refreshes highlighting fresh herbs and spices for spring/summer, and collaborations such as a limited-time terrace pairing with Veuve Clicquot.

staff_allergy_handling.text: Restaurant listing guidance indicates food allergies and disliked ingredients should be communicated in advance, and requests made on the day of the visit may not be accommodatable.

positives.text: CHOMPOO offers a dedicated multi-course vegan tasting menu (6 to 8 dishes) made only from seasonal vegetables, fruits, beans and herbs with no animal products — including appetizers, a Kao Yam herb salad, soup, a warm main, and plant-based dessert with tea.
The restaurant is additive-free and MSG-free across its menu.

cultural_comfort.note: Sits inside the very tourist-trafficked Shibuya PARCO complex near Shibuya Scramble, so basic English support and card payment are likely, but the menu, reservation platforms (Ikyu, OZmall, Hot Pepper) and course descriptions found are all in Japanese.

tokyo_peace_table_shibuya_doge.gf_detail: Not a dedicated gluten-free kitchen and no official allergen/cross-contamination statement was found. However, the plant-based, largely Italian/Ayurveda-influenced menu (no traditional soy-sauce/dashi-based Japanese cooking) reduces typical wheat-via-shoyu risk, and at least one diner reported being served fresh, soft gluten-free bread as part of a standard course, suggesting gluten-free substitutions are available. Celiac travelers should confirm cross-contamination handling directly with staff before dining.
tokyo_peace_table_shibuya_doge.vegan_detail: Entirely vegan kitchen (no meat, fish, dairy, or eggs). Being an Ayurveda/Italian-leaning concept rather than a traditional Japanese kitchen, it does not rely on katsuo/bonito dashi. The set courses are built around vegetables, curry, and pasta, with a reviewer noting the meal was explicitly dairy-free — unusual and deliberate given Ayurvedic cooking often defaults to dairy (ghee).

chef_bio.origin: Tokyo

The restaurant was later renovated to build out a full Ayurveda program, developed with input from Dr. Kazuo Uemba, described in press coverage as a leading figure in Japanese Ayurveda.
chef_bio.philosophy: The name PEACE TABLE expresses the idea that people can share good food and a moment of peace regardless of nationality, religion or skin color; the restaurant's peace-sign logo doubles as the "V" of "vegan. "
chef_bio.specialty: A personalized Ayurveda-based vegan set course: guests fill out a dosha questionnaire (Vata / Pitta / Kapha) and are served a matching course of soup, bread, salad, main and dessert — for example a creamy mushroom-and-truffle pasta on the Kapha menu.

anecdotes.text: Guests are given a warming Agni drink to aid digestion while completing a dosha questionnaire (an English version is available), then receive a course tailored to their result — one visitor's Kapha-type meal came with a creamy mushroom truffle pasta and a gluten-free bread described as fresh and soft.

gf_cross_contamination.text: A visiting food blogger noted her Kapha-type set course came with gluten-free bread that was "super fresh and soft," though no formal cross-contamination or dedicated-equipment statement was found.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Described as a fully vegan restaurant serving Ayurveda-style meals without dairy (notable since traditional Ayurvedic cooking often uses ghee/dairy), suggesting deliberate control over animal-derived ingredients.

staff_allergy_handling.text: On arrival, guests fill out a dosha (constitution) questionnaire — an English version is available — and staff/kitchen tailor the course to the guest's answers, which provides a natural touchpoint to flag allergies or gluten-free needs.

positives.text: 100% vegan, personalized menu system with an English questionnaire and a welcome digestive (Agni) drink before the meal.

cultural_comfort.note: An English-language dosha questionnaire and personalized menu guidance are offered, making the concept accessible to non-Japanese-speaking diners even though it requires more explanation than an average restaurant.

tokyo_tokyo_mercato_tokyo_dome.vegan_detail: No dedicated vegan menu was found. Every dish is served with a fresh vegetable salad side, and vegetable-topped pizzas/pastas exist on the menu, but cheese, butter, and animal stock are standard in the kitchen and no source confirms dairy-free preparation. Vegetarians could likely find something with cheese; strict vegans would need to ask staff carefully about hidden animal products.

The space is built around the concept of a Mercato (Italian market), pairing the pizzeria with an illy espresso bar and sommelier-recommended wines so guests can sample multiple facets of Italian food culture in one visit.

cultural_comfort.note: Sits inside the Tokyo Dome City shopping/entertainment complex, a heavily tourist-trafficked area, so basic English signage and picture menus are likely, though full English service is not confirmed.

tokyo_texmex_factory_shibuya_k.vegan_detail: Weekday lunch and the regular taco line-up include a plant-based 'Veggie Meat' (ベジタブルミート) taco option alongside the meat tacos, and make-your-own fajitas let diners skip meat and load up on guacamole, pico de gallo and beans. anecdotes.text: A visitor report described lines forming before opening on weekdays in Shibuya for the ¥1,380 all-you-can-eat taco/taco-rice lunch, noting the festive pink-and-skull decor as a highlight of the visit.

A local Shibuya gourmet write-up described the restaurant as offering an authentic-feeling Mexican dining experience just a short walk from the station, citing the imported decor and taco/fajita/burrito line-up.

positives.text: Corn tortillas (naturally gluten-free) are offered as an alternative to wheat 'flower' tortillas across the taco menu.
A plant-based 'Veggie Meat' taco/lunch option is listed alongside the meat-based tacos, giving vegetarians a menu item that doesn't require special requests.

cultural_comfort.note: A high-volume Tex-Mex chain restaurant a few minutes from Shibuya Station with an English-language Tabelog listing and a picture-heavy taco/fajita menu, so ordering should be manageable with basic gestures even without shared language.

chef_bio.background: Chat Gatto opened in 2016, run by a husband-and-wife chef duo: Takashi, who trained in Italian cooking, and Yoshiko, who trained in French cooking. chef_bio.philosophy: Home-style French and Italian cooking centered on vin nature (natural wine) and ingredients shipped directly from Ehime Prefecture — vegetables and seafood from the owner's native Imabari/Shimanami area, plus local poultry, pork, venison and wild boar.

Menu highlights spotted by diners include Ehime vegetable and fish marinades, a charcuterie platter, roasted wild boar, and tajarin with gold sesame and anchovy.

cultural_comfort.note: A small, reservation-recommended neighborhood bistro in a back alley with no confirmed English menu or English-speaking service, so a translation app or basic Japanese will help.

chef_bio.background: Nibo-shi Chuka Soba Suzuran is a niboshi (dried-sardine) ramen specialty shop near Shinjuku Sanchome Station, run by the INGS restaurant group, which operates several Tokyo ramen brands including Raa Men Hayashida.
chef_bio.philosophy: The shop aims for a niboshi broth with little of the bitterness (エグ味) that puts off people who usually dislike dried-sardine ramen, so the flavor stays refined, balanced, and clean-finishing despite its richness.
chef_bio.specialty: 濃厚煮干中華そば (rich niboshi ramen) and つけ麺 (tsukemen), made with a triple soup combining tonkotsu (pork bone), chicken, and dried-sardine (niboshi) dashi, topped with low-temperature-cooked rare chashu; noodles come in a choice of medium-thick curly or low-hydration thin styles.

anecdotes.text: The shop periodically runs a quantity-limited special, 特製炭火焼鯵煮干そば (charcoal-grilled horse mackerel niboshi soba), alongside its regular tsukemen.

gf_cross_contamination.text: No allergen or gluten-free accommodations were found in any source; this is a conventional wheat-noodle ramen shop where cross-contact with wheat is presumed throughout (shared broth pots, shared noodle-boiling water, shoyu-based tare).

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The shop's ramen and tsukemen use a shoyu/tare-seasoned niboshi-tonkotsu-chicken soup, and standard Japanese soy sauce contains wheat; no wheat-free soy sauce was mentioned.

vegan_cross_contact.text: The signature soup is a triple stock of pork bone (tonkotsu), chicken, and dried sardine (niboshi), with no vegetarian or vegan broth option mentioned anywhere.

cultural_comfort.note: A standard neighborhood ramen counter shop with no indication of English menus or English-speaking service, so expect Japanese-only ordering (likely point-and-order or simple counter service).

Not suitable for celiac or strict gluten-free diners.

chef_bio.origin: Nishi-Shinjuku, Tokyo
chef_bio.background: Opened February 8, 1999. It began life as one of the licensed "Jiro Foods System" (フーズ系) satellite shops operating under the Jiro name but outside the founder's direct lineage. After Ramen Jiro's trademark was formally registered in 2003, most of these satellite shops were forced to rebrand or fold — leaving only the Kanda shop as a lingering Foods-kei holdout — and the Kotakibashi-dori shop transitioned to direct management under Jiro headquarters.
chef_bio.specialty: Standard Jiro-style ramen: thick wheat noodles in a soy-sauce (shoyu) pork-bone broth, piled with cabbage, bean sprouts, and thick-cut chashu, customizable via the shop's shouted "call" system (garlic, vegetables, pork fat, sauce). Unusually for a Jiro shop it also offers table seating and a cheaper "student ramen. "

anecdotes.text: During its years as a Foods-kei satellite the shop had a rocky reputation and was jokingly nicknamed "the worst Jiro" among devoted fans (ジロリアン); its standing has since recovered, with reports of the recipe improving further around 2017 and the noodles becoming noticeably thicker around 2019.
Unlike most Jiro shops, which are counter-only, this location has a 4-person and a 2-person table alongside its 12-seat counter.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Extremely small, single-line open kitchen where noodles, broth, and toppings for every order pass through the same equipment — no separated prep area exists for allergen-sensitive orders.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The tare/soup is described as a soy-sauce (shoyu) based, micro-emulsified broth with a pronounced soy sauce character — standard Japanese soy sauce contains wheat.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Broth is a pork-bone (tonkotsu) base simmered with pork, and standard bowls are topped with generous chashu pork and often pork back fat (abura); no plant-based broth or protein option is offered.

cultural_comfort.note: Ramen Jiro shops run on an unwritten etiquette and a shouted "call" system for customizing toppings (garlic, vegetables, oil, sauce) that can feel intimidating without some Japanese-language prep, though many foreign fans do fine with a quick primer beforehand.

tokyo_kohikan_shibuya.gf_detail: No gluten-free menu, wheat-free labeling, dedicated fryer, or wheat-free soy sauce was mentioned in any source. tokyo_kohikan_shibuya.vegan_detail: No vegan-labeled dishes were found. chef_bio.background: Ra-men Hosenka opened on July 26, 2018 in Kabukicho, Shinjuku, as a sister shop to the ramen brands 煮干中華そば鈴蘭 (Niboshi Chuka Soba Suzuran) and らぁ麺はやし田 (Ra-men Hayashida), all operated by the restaurant company INGS Co. , Ltd. (founded 2009), which runs seven ramen shops plus the Italian restaurant chain CONA. Within the INGS ramen family, each shop has its own broth identity — Suzuran is dried-sardine (niboshi) based, Hayashida is chicken based, and Hosenka is the group's seafood-based shop, built around kinmedai (golden-eye snapper).
chef_bio.philosophy: The kitchen keeps no condiments on the tables, asking diners to taste the kinmedai broth exactly as the chef intends rather than adjust it themselves; the shop is also promoted as 無化調 (no added MSG), extracting its umami from the fish bones alone.
chef_bio.specialty: Kinmedai ramen (金目鯛らぁ麺) — a light, shio-style bowl made from a dashi of kinmedai and madai (sea bream) bones, extracted with careful temperature and time control to keep the broth delicate rather than heavy. The chashu is sous-vide pork shoulder loin served rare for a moist, tender texture, topped with two large, crisp menma shoots. For an extra ¥200, diners can finish the meal with kinmedai chazuke, pouring the remaining dashi over rice.

anecdotes.text: 店内には卓上調味料がなく、スープや具材へのこだわりが徹底されています (There are no condiments on the tables — the shop is thoroughly committed to its soup and toppings as prepared).

鯛塩系のラーメン...最後に金目鯛茶漬けで二度オイシイ (A tai-shio style ramen finished, for an extra charge, with kinmedai chazuke for a second course).

vegan_cross_contact.text: The signature broth is a kinmedai/madai fish-bone dashi and the standard topping is pork chashu, so the dish itself is built on fish and meat, not merely at risk of cross-contact.

positives.text: The shop advertises itself as 無化調 (no added MSG), sourcing its umami from kinmedai/madai bones alone rather than seasoning additives.

cultural_comfort.note: Ordering is by ticket machine, payment is cash-only, and no English menu is documented, so some comfort with Japanese-style ramen-shop customs (or willingness to point/gesture) is helpful.

The restaurant's tempura is plated separately from the soba so it stays crisp, meant to be eaten first with a touch of rock salt before the noodles are dipped in the broth.

chef_bio.origin: Nihonbashi, Tokyo
chef_bio.background: Katsukichi opened in 1962 near Korakuen/Tokyo Dome and has kept its retro Showa-era interior almost unchanged ever since. The founder, Yoshida Kichizaemon, was the son of Iwatani Shohei, a well-known Meiji-era tobacco magnate. The dining room is filled with roughly 2,000 antiques — Imari porcelain tableware and reclaimed wood and water pipes salvaged from the old Tamagawa Canal — giving it the feel of a small private museum.
chef_bio.philosophy: A craftsman's commitment to quality ingredients — branded pork, fresh breadcrumbs, and fresh oil — carried forward largely unchanged since the shop's founding over 60 years ago.
chef_bio.specialty: Tonkatsu made from select branded domestic pork fillet, hand-coated in fresh nama-panko breadcrumbs and slowly fried in fresh corn oil; also known for a steak served with a distinctive soy-sauce-based sauce rather than the usual demi-glace.

anecdotes.text: Novelist Yukio Mishima, who trained at a nearby gym in Korakuen, was a regular. According to a well-known story, when a steak he ordered wasn't cooked the way he liked, he sent it back untouched and left without eating — and his preference for soy sauce over the restaurant's original demi-glace sauce is said to be the origin of the soy-sauce steak that later became a house specialty.
Author Yasunari Kawabata, a close acquaintance of the founder, gifted the restaurant a calligraphy work reading '亥' (boar), which is still displayed on the restaurant's wood paneling today.

cultural_comfort.note: A historic, traditional Japanese tonkatsu restaurant with a retro Showa-era atmosphere and antique-filled dining room; no English menu was confirmed, so a little Japanese or pointing at the picture menu may help.

It is widely credited in Tokyo food writing as the birthplace of ten-tama soba — soba topped with tempura and a soft egg — and has since grown into a small group of standing soba counters across Tokyo (Kanda, Okachimachi, Shimbashi, Ginza) while its original Shinjuku counter keeps running nearly around the clock.
chef_bio.philosophy: Fast, no-frills soba built for standing-counter speed, carried by a deeply concentrated soy-based tsuyu broth the shop has refined for over 50 years.
chef_bio.specialty: 元祖天玉そば (Ganso Ten-tama Soba) — soba topped with freshly fried kakiage tempura and a soft hot-spring egg

anecdotes.text: Kameya is credited as the originator of ten-tama soba, topping kakiage tempura with a soft-cooked hot-spring egg instead of a raw one — a combination now considered a Tokyo standing-soba classic.
The Shinjuku shop has no doors or walls, built like an open-air stall — a look it has kept for more than 50 years since opening in 1971.
The shop's dark, richly concentrated soba tsuyu is a deliberate house style, giving even a hurried standing-counter meal deep, memorable flavor.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Standing (tachigui) soba shops like this one typically raise the wheat-flour ratio in their noodles so the strands hold up to fast prep and handling — the soba here is not a low-gluten or gluten-free product.

chef_bio.origin: Asakusa, Tokyo (site southeast of Sensō-ji Temple)
chef_bio.background: The restaurant occupies a building that has kept its Shōwa-era (mid-20th-century) street-front appearance. It previously operated under the related name たつみ屋 (Tatsumiya) and reopened as にょろ助 東南屋 浅草 on November 11, 2006, run by the Tokyo restaurant group 際コーポレーション (Kiwa Corporation), which operates a small number of similarly branded 'Nyorosuke' eel/loach restaurants. The shop's name, 東南屋, literally 'southeast house,' refers to its position southeast of Sensō-ji Temple and is read 'Tatsumiya' as a nod to the old zodiac-direction name for that compass point.
chef_bio.philosophy: Keeps old shitamachi (downtown Asakusa) dining traditions alive by serving unagi, dojō (loach), tempura, and sukiyaki together under one roof, in a room with sunken-kotatsu tatami seating reminiscent of an earlier era.
chef_bio.specialty: 地焼きうなぎ (jiyaki-style grilled eel) — eel grilled directly without pre-steaming, a Kansai-region technique that yields a crisp exterior, tender flesh, and more pronounced eel flavor than the steamed Kantō style; also known for どぜう鍋 (Asakusa-style loach hot pot), a downtown Edo-period commoners' dish served heaped with scallions.

anecdotes.text: The restaurant's jiyaki grilling method — grilling the eel without pre-steaming — is a distinctly Kansai technique, said to give the eel a crisper bite, tender flesh, and stronger aroma than the more common steamed Kantō style.

The shop's name, Tōnan-ya (東南屋), refers to its location southeast of Sensō-ji Temple and is read 'Tatsumiya,' echoing the old zodiac-direction name for that compass point; the restaurant previously traded under the related name Tatsumiya before rebranding as にょろ助 東南屋 in 2006.

roles: Live seafood (活魚) specialty restaurant, part of Eiwa Group
chef_bio.background: いけす無門 新宿 is operated by Eiwa Group (永和グループ), a Tokyo restaurant company also known for its 月亭 shabu-shabu brand. The Shinjuku Kabukicho location is built around a giant in-house fish tank (いけす) at the center of the dining room, with counter seats overlooking it on the first floor and private tatami/horigotatsu rooms upstairs and in a waterfall-accented basement floor.
chef_bio.philosophy: The restaurant's concept centers on 活魚 (live fish) cooked to order: fish, spiny lobster and abalone are sourced daily from regions across Japan and kept alive in the tank until a customer orders, so the seafood served is caught and prepared within minutes rather than pre-cut.
chef_bio.specialty: 泳ぎいか (live squid sashimi) — squid kept swimming in the tank until ordered, then hand-cut to order by the chef.

anecdotes.text: The restaurant's official site notes that freshly caught live squid has a distinctive semi-translucent appearance rather than plain white, and that this freshness is what gives it its characteristic sweetness and texture — a point of pride the restaurant highlights as its signature dish.

chef_bio.origin: 新潟県 (Niigata Prefecture)
chef_bio.background: Founder and president Takahashi Yuka grew up in Niigata eating a local specialty: ramen made with yakiago (grilled flying fish) dashi. Wanting to bring that hometown flavor to Tokyo, she founded the company in 2011 and, with no prior experience in the ramen industry, opened the first shop as a two-person, husband-and-wife operation in Myogadani in 2012. Business was slow at first, but after the shop relocated/expanded to a spot in Kabukicho, Shinjuku in February 2015, it became an instant hit — the store is widely credited with popularizing yakiago (grilled flying fish) ramen as a nationwide trend when the ingredient was previously little known. The brand celebrated its 10th anniversary in February 2025 and has since grown into a small multi-location company.
chef_bio.philosophy: Recreate and share a nostalgic, hometown Niigata flavor — yakiago-based ramen — with Tokyo diners, elevating a regional ingredient that was largely unknown in the capital before this shop popularized it.
chef_bio.specialty: 焼きあご塩らー麺 (Yakiago Shio Ramen) — a salt ramen built on a broth of pork bone and chicken carcass stock combined with grilled flying fish (yakiago), dried sardines (niboshi), and kelp, finished with a proprietary flavored oil that concentrates the grilled-fish aroma. The noodles are a hand-kneaded style made from premium center-cut wheat flour co-developed with a long-established Kyoto noodle maker, and the tare (sauce base) uses Sekigahara tamari soy sauce paired with a generous amount of dried sardines.

anecdotes.text: Takahashi started the company in 2011 with no ramen-industry background, opening a small husband-and-wife shop in Myogadani in 2012 that struggled with slow business before finding success after moving into Kabukicho in 2015.
The Kabukicho shop is credited with sparking the modern 'yakiago (grilled flying fish) ramen' boom in Tokyo, and the brand marked its 10th anniversary in February 2025.

chef_bio.chef_name: Koichi Murata (founder, 1973); now run by second-generation owner Shinsuke Murata
chef_bio.origin: Founded in 1973 (Showa 48) in Kanda-Jimbocho by Koichi Murata, who had previously run an earlier curry shop called Indira in Takashimadaira, Tokyo.
chef_bio.background: In his twenties Murata traveled to France, ostensibly to study art, and ended up spending several years there. He worked in a friend's restaurant, where he became captivated by the depth and technique of classic French brown sauce (sauce espagnole/demi-glace). Bringing that sauce-making tradition back to Japan and folding it into curry produced what he named '欧風カレー' (European-style curry).
chef_bio.philosophy: Murata summed up his curry as 'the aroma of India, the taste of Europe' — rather than a straightforward Indian-style curry, the sauce is built like a French brown sauce: butter-and-flour roux simmered for hours with beef or pork stock, wine, and fruit and vegetables cooked down slowly in butter, giving a rounder, less fiery, dairy-rich flavor with sweetness balancing the spice.
chef_bio.specialty: European-style beef or pork curry, served with a whole boiled potato and a pat of butter presented separately on its own plate before the curry arrives.

anecdotes.text: Murata spent several formative years in France in his twenties; what began as an art-study trip turned into an apprenticeship of sorts in a friend's restaurant kitchen, where he fell for the depth of French brown sauce and later built Bondy's curry around it.

Bondy is credited as the Jimbocho curry shop that first served a whole boiled potato alongside the curry. In an interview, second-generation owner Shinsuke Murata explained his father served the potato first, echoing the 'first course' convention of the French meals he had trained on.

Before founding Bondy, Murata had run an earlier, lesser-known curry shop called 'Indira' in Takashimadaira, Tokyo — part of the winding path from Itabashi to Jimbocho that curry historians trace for the shop.

chef_bio.specialty: 創業つけめん (Sōgyō Tsukemen / "Founding Tsukemen") — a revival of a recipe Rokurinsha served for only one month back at its 2005 opening and later brought back as a legendary 'phantom' dish; it pairs a rich double soup of chicken-and-pork stock with seafood dashi, sharpened with a soy-based tare and a house spice blend.

anecdotes.text: The founding tsukemen recipe was served for just one month in 2005 at Rokurinsha's original Osaki shop and gained cult status as a 'phantom' menu item before Sharin brought it back; it has since sold over 200,000 bowls chain-wide.

chef_bio.background: haishop cafe is run by Innovation Design Inc. , founded by Tarō Ishizeki. The company opened its first omiyage (souvenir) shop and restaurants in 2019, then pivoted fully toward sustainability in early 2020 after the founder saw how normalized sustainable living had become while visiting New York. The Shibuya Scramble Square branch opened on the 7th floor in September 2022, directly connected to Shibuya Station.
chef_bio.philosophy: The concept is "solving social issues through food": ingredients are chosen with attention to environment, sourcing, and social impact, and the cafe welcomes vegan and vegetarian diners with a menu that is roughly 80% vegan. Customers who bring their own tumbler or container get 100 yen off drinks.
chef_bio.specialty: Soy-meat vegan burger and a vegan tartare bagel sandwich, alongside all-vegan soft-serve ice cream and seasonal fresh smoothies.

anecdotes.text: haishop cafe's operator, Innovation Design, was reported as the first in Japan to receive a three-star rating from the Sustainable Restaurant Association (Japan) for its sustainability practices, around the time the Shibuya Scramble Square branch opened with its 80%-vegan menu.

The brand's shift to a sustainability-first business came after the founder's trip to New York, where sustainable living felt normalized; back in Japan at the start of 2020 the company decided to reorient the business around sustainability.

Coffee itself is vegan, but the food menu is not.

chef_bio.origin: Kanda-Jimbocho, Chiyoda-ku, Tokyo

The founding couple's daughter, Miwa Tokuko, is now the second-generation owner, carrying on the taste and atmosphere passed down from her parents for nearly half a century.
chef_bio.philosophy: A family-run, old-fashioned kissaten (Showa-retro coffee shop) philosophy centered on preserving the original recipes and unhurried atmosphere of the founders rather than chasing trends.
chef_bio.specialty: Gratin toast (グラタントースト), the signature dish since the shop's founding; also known for a mackerel-and-vegetable curry toast sandwich and, more recently, an ogura (red bean) butter toast served with coffee.

anecdotes.text: The shop's name, Trois Bagues, is French for "three rings" (trois = three, bague = ring) — a direct translation of the owner family's surname Miwa (三輪, literally "three wheels/rings"), and is also meant to evoke the connection between customer, staff, and coffee cup.
Second-generation owner Miwa Tokuko continues to run the cafe, having inherited it from her parents who opened it in 1976.

cultural_comfort.note: A classic old-school Japanese kissaten with a Japanese-only menu and no particular English support, though its long-running fame in the bookstore district means walk-in visitors are common.

chef_bio.origin: Nakatsugawa, Gifu Prefecture (Ohashi Farm)
chef_bio.background: 農おおはし is a producer-run izakaya connected to Ohashi Farm (大橋農園), an actual working farm in Nakatsugawa City, Gifu Prefecture. The restaurant describes itself as a bridge between farmers and diners: it runs its own agriculture and livestock operation, sources seasonal vegetables directly from the family farm, and frames its mission around raising the standing of producers and giving diners traceability they can trust.
chef_bio.philosophy: Build a direct line from a real farm to the plate — showcasing seasonal, farm-grown vegetables in simple preparations (salads, tempura) alongside creative cooked dishes, paired with a curated list of organic wine, sake, and shochu.
chef_bio.specialty: Seasonal vegetable tempura (旬の野菜天ぷら) and vegetable-forward dishes such as colorful seasonal salads and a farmer's meat-and-vegetable stir-fry

anecdotes.text: The Ohashi family's farming story goes back to wartime hardship, when the current farm's founder's grandmother, Masako Ohashi, began growing a fiery heirloom chili called ajime pepper (あじめこしょう) — a variety cultivated in the same corner of Gifu for roughly 400 years. She called it a kind of 'magic powder,' saying even a pinch could turn a poor wartime meal into something delicious; the farm still grows it today alongside corn, broccoli, garlic, and sweet potatoes that supply the Tokyo restaurant.

positives.text: The restaurant's own description emphasizes fresh, seasonal vegetables shipped directly from its affiliated Ohashi Farm in Gifu, forming the base of colorful salads, vegetable tempura, and other vegetable-centered dishes, which gives naturally plant-forward options on the menu even though it is not a dedicated vegan restaurant.

chef_bio.background: An 80-plus-year-old neighborhood soba shop tucked in the basement at the very entrance of Shibuya Center-gai, just past the Scramble Crossing. anecdotes.text: Located at the entrance of Center-gai in the basement of a building across from Mizuho Bank, the shop is often described as an island of calm below the crowds and noise of one of Shibuya's busiest streets.
The shop has been serving its Sarashina-style noodles for over 60-80 years, adjusting flour selection and dough hydration daily according to the season and weather.

chef_bio.background: The shop's roots trace back to 1455, when the warlord Ota Dokan, while building Edo Castle, held a moon-viewing party at Takaido and was presented with hand-formed dango by a local family — he loved them so much he kept requesting them. The name 'Oiwake' (追分) refers to the fork in old Naito-Shinjuku where the Koshu Kaido and Ome Kaido roads split, a busy travelers' crossroads. In the summer of 1947, just after the war, founder Fujii Toemon opened a small shop called 'Yanagiya' in Shinjuku Sanchome; having heard the old story of Oiwake dango from town elders, he set out to revive its taste on the very spot where the roads once met, and the business grew into today's Oiwake Dango Honpo.
chef_bio.philosophy: Dough, red bean paste, and beans are all hand-prepared fresh in the shop's own kitchen every morning before the dango are made and sold the same day.
chef_bio.specialty: Otona no Mitarashi (大人のみたらし, "Adult's Mitarashi") — dango glazed in the shop's mitarashi sauce blended with sansho pepper and fresh shichimi spice, giving the classic sweet-salty soy glaze a warmer, spicier edge.

anecdotes.text: 太田道灌が江戸城築城中、高井戸で中秋の名月の宴を開いた際、地元の名族が手づくりの団子を献上し、道灌がその味をいたく気に入って以後も所望した、という室町時代の逸話が「追分だんご」の起源とされる。
終戦間もない1947年夏、新宿三丁目に「やなぎ家」という白い暖簾を掲げたのが現在の追分だんご本舗の始まり。創業者・藤井藤右ヱ門が町の古老から追分だんごの由来を聞き、新宿追分の地でその味を復活させようとしたという。
名物「大人のみたらし」は山椒と生七味を効かせた甘辛いタレが特徴で、起源は室町時代にまで遡ると紹介されている。
